title: AutoSynthesis: An agentic system for automated meta-analysis
author: Moein Taherinezhad, Sebastian Maier, Gerardo Vitagliano, Francesco Pierri, Stefan Feuerriegel
raw_text: Evidence synthesis is crucial for turning primary research into reliable knowledge for science, medicine, education, and policy. Yet, quantitative evidence synthesis remains largely manual and difficult to scale. Here, we introduce AutoSynthesis, an end-to-end multi-agent system for automated meta-analysis. Given a research question in natural language, AutoSynthesis formulates a search strategy, retrieves scientific literature, screens candidate studies, assesses full-text eligibility, extracts quantitative statistics, computes standardized effect sizes, and finally performs random-effects meta-analysis. AutoSynthesis further supports heterogeneity analysis to examine how effect sizes vary across moderators, as well as risk-of-bias assessment. As output, AutoSynthesis produces a transparent report aligned with PRISMA guidelines. In our application, AutoSynthesis screened over 28 studies and extracted more than 20 quantitative claims. The pooled effect estimates produced by AutoSynthesis are similar to Hedges' $g$ of expert-conducted meta-analyses, indicating close agreement with manual evidence synthesis. Together, these results show that AutoSynthesis can make quantitative evidence synthesis more scalable, thereby supporting evidence-based decision-making across disciplines.
summary: This paper introduces autosynthesis, a multi-agent system designed to automate meta-analysis, which is the process of systematically combining results from multiple studies to draw stronger conclusions. traditionally, this is a very manual and time-consuming task. autosynthesis uses several collaborating ai agents to handle different stages, such as formulating search strategies, retrieving scientific literature, screening studies, and extracting data, all initiated by a natural language research question. for you, this is an excellent example of how complex problems can be broken down and tackled by multiple, specialized ai agents working together. it highlights advanced applications of llms and agentic systems, similar to sophisticated rag pipelines. you could study the paper to understand how different agents are designed and how they coordinate tasks in a complex workflow.
why: Demonstrates multi-agent systems automating complex research, applying advanced RAG principles.

title: Ask HN: How useful is Gemini for Google Apps?

raw_text: I recently wrote a Google doc to describe a presentation. I press the magic Gemini button. After some preamble prompt BS, I paste my "Slides" document content, and ask it to create me some slides.Gemini (paraphrasing): "Oh, sorry, I can only work on one slide at a time".WTF? I go to a different frontier LLM, I ask it to make me a PPTX file from my description (which I downloaded from Google docs as markdown). After a few minutes I have a nice PPTX file. There must be a better way! Please help me HN.I'm also keen to hear what are some actual cool tricks that do work with Gemini and/or frustrations others have had. Let loose.

title: Salesforce Messaging Architecture: Platform Events, Async Sends, and Multi-Tenancy at Scale
author: Devam Gupta
raw_text: Most enterprise messaging integrations function as external connectors. They reside outside the Customer Relationship Management (CRM) platform, receive webhooks, write peripheral logs, and consider the process integrated. Consequently, messages are isolated within the messaging platform while CRM records remain strictly inside the CRM, bridged only by fragile sync jobs, rigid field mappings, and eventual consistency windows. This paper outlines an alternative architectural paradigm: constructing the entire messaging core natively inside the CRM. Within this model, every message is treated as a native CRM record,every outbound path is a platform-native transaction, and all state parameters - including delivery status, opt-in metrics, conversation history, and record ownership - are stored as standard database objects. This structural native alignment allows the system to utilize standard reporting pipelines, operate inside native workflow builders, and trigger platform automation seamlessly. Drawing from a production managed package deployed across independent enterprise organizations spanning healthcare, sales operations, field services, and customer support, this study evaluates the core design patterns, platform scaling mechanics, multi-tenant decoupling constraints, and the boundaries of the platform-native architectural design.
summary: This paper outlines how salesforce manages messaging within its platform, focusing on platform events, asynchronous communication, and multi-tenancy at scale. It contrasts this with traditional methods where messaging systems are often separate, leading to data silos. Salesforce's approach integrates messaging deeply, aiming for greater consistency and efficiency. As an aspiring SDE/SWE, understanding robust, scalable messaging architectures is fundamental. Your AI/ML models will often be part of larger systems needing efficient communication. This offers insights into designing systems that handle high loads and maintain data consistency, valuable for building resilient full-stack or MLOps solutions. You could consider how such a system handles data flowing into an MLOps pipeline or triggers AI model inferences.
why: Teaches scalable, robust messaging architecture, essential for building reliable full-stack and MLOps systems.

title: Can LLMs Write Reliable Rubrics? A Meta-Evaluation for Experiment Reproduction
author: Hanhua Hong, Yizhi Li, Jiaoyan Chen, Luu Gia Huy, Sophia Ananiadou, Jung-jae Kim, Chenghua Lin
raw_text: Rubric-based evaluation is a promising approach for assessing open-ended outputs from LLM-based research agents, particularly in paper reproduction, where direct paper-to-repository comparison is prone to hallucination. However, constructing paper-specific rubrics requires substantial expert effort, limiting the scalability of benchmarks such as PaperBench. In this work, we present, to our knowledge, the first systematic meta-evaluation of LLM-generated rubrics for paper reproduction. We reformulate rubrics into a checklist-style format and evaluate four generation settings across two backbone models. We meta-evaluate generated rubrics intrinsically by semantic similarity and extrinsically by score alignment with ground-truth rubrics. Our results show that the augmented settings substantially improves downstream evaluation alignment, with the strongest setting approaching the human baseline, while intrinsic gains are more modest. Further analyses reveal that LLM-generated rubrics are often overly fine-grained, biased toward high scores, and less adaptive to paper domains, highlighting both the affordances and limitations.
summary: this research paper explores whether large language models (llms) can reliably generate rubrics, which are scoring guides, for evaluating the open-ended outputs of other llm-based research agents. it's a 'meta-evaluation' because it assesses the llm's ability to create the tools used for evaluation, particularly in the context of reproducing scientific papers. for you, this is significant because evaluating llm outputs, especially for complex or creative tasks, is a major challenge in ai development. if llms can help create reliable evaluation rubrics, it could greatly scale up the benchmarking and development of new ai agents, which is crucial for r&d and mlops. when working on your own llm projects, consider how an llm might assist you in defining success criteria or generating test cases for open-ended tasks.
why: explores using llms to create evaluation rubrics, improving ai agent assessment.

title: Decomposing Runtime, Kernel, and Quantization Speedups via a Matched FP16 Intermediate: A Hardware-Conditioned Case Study on Four NVIDIA RTX A5000 GPUs
author: Weijia Han, Lisha Qu
raw_text: Reported serving speedups from quantized kernels typically bundle the weight format, the kernel, and the inference runtime into one number. We present an attribution study on four NVIDIA RTX A5000 GPUs, 24 GiB each, on a single host with NVLink-bridged pairs. A matched intermediate stack that keeps the faster runtime without the quantized kernel splits the full speedup into a runtime part and a kernel and quantization part. Under matched greedy decoding the full stack reaches $2.58\times$ end to end, with the runtime change accounting for about two thirds of that gain on a logarithmic scale; across three similar model families the kernel and quantization part moves by at most 1.5%. Sharding one instance across all four cards falls well below doubling: a profiler trace attributes about 80% of the per token shortfall to coordination, and an NVLink versus PCIe control on the same hardware shows similar realized bandwidth on both links, pointing away from link bandwidth as the cause. Whether to run one sharded instance or several independent ones depends on the workload and the model, with the ranking reversing on the larger model: the smaller model splits between sharding and multiple instances by workload, while the larger model favors two paired instances on every workload. Quantization extends sustainable concurrent users roughly four times past a reproducible half precision memory cliff. Differences in sampling mode and prompt pool between the two stacks are documented as threats to validity.
summary: This paper looks at how we measure the speed improvements when we use quantized models, especially on GPUs like the NVIDIA RTX A5000. Often, when you hear about a model running faster due to quantization, that single speedup number actually combines several factors: the way the model's weights are stored (like 8-bit integers instead of 16-bit floats), the specific optimized code (kernel) that runs these operations, and the overall inference runtime. The researchers here tried to separate these factors. They found a way to isolate the speedup from the runtime itself versus the speedup from the specialized quantized kernels. This helps us understand exactly where the performance gains come from. For you, understanding these components is crucial for optimizing your own LLM deployments. You could try to profile your own quantized models to see if the speedup is more from runtime efficiencies or the quantization itself.
why: Understand where LLM inference speedups come from for better optimization.
